tier_reason: README benchstat tables compare the asm build against a naive byte loop and the uint64 purego build of the same functions, produced by the public benchmark.sh (go test -run=^# -count=10 -bench, then -tags purego, then the *Naive benchmarks) over and_test.go, any_test.go, any_masked_test.go and popcnt_test.go; CPU models are printed (13th Gen Intel Core i9-13900, Apple M2 Pro) and the compiler is the Go gc toolchain with default go test flags. The Go toolchain version is not recorded (go.mod requires go 1.24.0), which is the one soft spot for A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go gc toolchain with default go test flags; exact commands in benchmark.sh (go test -run=^# -count=10 -bench='^Benchmark(And|Or|Xor|AndNot|Any|AnyMasked|Popcnt|PopcntMasked)$', the same with -tags purego, and the *Naive benchmarks), compared with benchstat@latest. Go version not printed in the README output; go.mod and internal/asm/go.mod require go 1.24.0 (the Popcnt benchmarks use b.Loop, which needs Go 1.24+).
corrections.caveats: Baseline is a deliberately naive byte loop; the stronger comparison is the uint64-wise purego column (derived from page data: asm about 7.8x faster than purego on And-32 2825.5ns vs 360.8ns, about 2.95x on Popcnt-32 66.45us vs 22.49us, geomean about 5.1x on the i9-13900 and about 4.6x on the M2 Pro). The amd64 AVX2 assembly is generated by avo programs in internal/asm (and_amd64.s carries a 'Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT' header); the arm64 NEON code in and_arm64.s is hand-written Go assembly. The and/or/xor/andnot/any benchmarks run on 32,000-byte buffers (a commit of 2024-08-04 moved to 32K buffers 'so we're less memory constrained'), so the 80+ GiB/s rows are cache-resident; popcount rows use 1,000,000-byte buffers; Any benchmarks use an all-zero buffer (full scan, worst case). The Apple M2 Pro table comes from an older run: it has a Memset row that the current benchmark.sh no longer runs and lacks the Any, AnyMasked and PopcntMasked rows. The baseline is Go gc output, not a C/C++ -O3 compiler, and the library is a Go package (not directly callable from C++). Very small repo (2 stars, 2 forks).

notes: All quoted numbers match the README benchstat tables exactly. Kept A on the public harness plus stated CPUs and default Go flags; the orchestrator may cap at C if a missing Go version counts as missing compiler information. Shortcomings: naive-loop baseline inflates the headline (purego column gives about 5x geomean), cache-resident 32 KB buffers, stale M2 table, Go-only library.

tier_reason: The repo README gives only the authors' own cycles-per-byte figures (all match the record) with no baseline row, no compiler, flags or board details, and the repo contains no benchmark harness (armcortexm/fixslicing holds only aes.h and .s files). The peer-reviewed TCHES 2021 comparison could not be opened (eprint.iacr.org, tches.iacr.org, artifacts.iacr.org and the rub.de mirror all fail DNS here), so the B lift stays pending.

corrections.caveats: Repo page gives only the authors' own cycle counts for non-unrolled code (the README says unrolling is slightly faster and refers to the paper); no baseline row, compiler, flags or benchmark harness in the repo. The comparison to earlier work is in the peer-reviewed TCHES 2021 issue 1 paper (pp. 402-425, ePrint 2020/1123, IACR artifact tches/2021/a6), which could not be opened here. Search snippets only: the TCHES abstract reports fixsliced AES-128 at 80 and 91 cycles per byte on ARM Cortex-M and E31 RISC-V with precomputed round keys, improving the previous records by 21% and 26% (the ePrint version says 80 and 87 cpb, 21% and 30%), and the CHES 2021 slides cite prior bitsliced AES-128 at 102 and 125 cpb. The baseline is earlier hand-written bitsliced AES, not compiler -O3 output or a stdlib, so it is off the category baseline. The C opt32 directory is didactic and not benchmarked. The masked implementation has no practical security evaluation (README caution) and its RNG code is specific to the STM32F407VG board.

notes: Numbers match the README; tier stays C and is a candidate for a paper-access retier to B once the TCHES paper or the IACR artifact page is reachable (abstract claims 21% and 26% over previous records, snippet only). Last commit 2024-10-17 (README update), so stale; 72 stars, MIT. Shortcomings: no baseline or methodology in the repo, off-category baseline (prior hand-written bitsliced AES).

tier_reason: The README lists only the project's own cycle counts (all match the record) and says it 'seems to be faster than' five AVR AES libraries and any pure C/C++ implementation without any competitor numbers. Public cycle-counting code exists (Timer1 measurements under AES_BENCHMARK in AVR-AES-Faster.ino plus AES_benchmark.S), but it times only this library; toolchain and flags are not stated.

corrections.hardware: 8-bit AVR, Arduino Uno (ATmega328P) test sketch; cycles counted with Timer1 under AES_BENCHMARK in AVR-AES-Faster.ino
corrections.caveats: The faster-than claims against named libraries carry no numbers on the page, and the bundled pure C implementation (TestAES.cpp) is used only as a key-expansion self-check, never timed. Cycle counts are for the inlined assembly with no rcall/ret; the README says the C ABI adds about 140 cycles per block on the callee side. Search snippet only: Osvik, Bos, Stefan and Canright (FSE 2010) report 124.6 and 181.3 cycles per byte on AVR, about 1994 and 2901 cycles per block (derived), so this library's flash-S-box AES-128 encryption at 2111 cycles is slower than that paper's figure and the RAM-S-box 1951 cycles only about 2% faster, while decryption (2527 to 2687 cycles) is faster; whether the paper's counts include call overhead or key handling could not be checked. Baseline libraries are other AVR assembly, not compiler output. Constant-time claim relies on AVR having no data cache (table lookups in flash or RAM).

notes: Numbers match the README; tier C confirmed. Main shortcoming: no competitor numbers anywhere in the repo, and a snippet-derived check against Osvik et al. suggests encryption is not faster with the flash S-box. 7 stars, MPL-2.0, last commit 2020-12-18 (abandoned).
